title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions

details.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
details.abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safetycritical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users’ legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe .

title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding

details.title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
details.abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely

details.title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely
details.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot’s other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.

title: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning

details.title: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning
details.abstract: SFT raises the accuracy of VideoLLMs, yet behind this rise the model increasingly relies on textual regularities of the training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. VETO suppresses this shortcut by projecting the fine-tuning update onto the orthogonal complement of the subspace the text alone occupies, so the model keeps the gains of SFT while grounding its answer in both the video and the text.

title: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests

details.title: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests
details.abstract: AI has made building a website change take minutes, but finding out whether customers like it still takes weeks of live testing. Squoosh simulates how people use a site, so teams can see what their customers will likely do before anything goes live. This paper is the proof. We took 318 real website A/B tests that had already finished, hid the results, and asked our model, UX-1, to pick the winner. It got 267 right (84%). The best general-purpose AI model we tried got 62%. Teams use this to check designs, find where customers get stuck, test pricing and offers, and pick which ideas are worth a live test.

title: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models

details.title: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models
details.abstract: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer’s evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, trainingfree inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target’s latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transitionaware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63× speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft’s 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.

details.title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
details.abstract: S1CogBench tests System One decision models, which return one fast typed decision over the legal options, on 24 established cognitive experiments (27 modes), with seven open models and the Jev API. Acting well does not imply predicting humans. In WCST, Nox has the highest autonomous accuracy among the evaluated models (32.1%) yet predicts held-out human choices worse than uniform choice. When more choices remain in the Horizon task, humans pick the less-observed arm 10.00 points more often, while the models predict changes of only -0.49 to 2.62 points. title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience

details.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
details.abstract: PlayCraft is an automated framework for designing engaging games that give players a path from beginner play to mastery. PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting: A player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. A crafter agent then uses the experience from the player agent to revise the game, aiming to reward better decisions and execution.
